name: Szent István Park and the Wallenberg Memorial
address: Szent István park, Újlipótváros riverside, Budapest XIII (between Újpesti rakpart and Hollán Ernő utca)
intro: Szent István park is a riverside park in Újlipótváros, in Budapest’s thirteenth district, looking across the Danube towards Margaret Island. It was laid out in the 1930s to designs by Béla Rerrich on the site of a former parquet factory. Among its memorials is a statue of Saint George raised in honour of Raoul Wallenberg.
about: Szent István park lies on the Danube side of Újlipótváros, at the western end of Csanády utca between Újpesti rakpart and Hollán Ernő utca. It takes its name from King Stephen I of Hungary and looks across the river to Margaret Island. According to the district’s own introduction, it was created where a parquet factory had stood.

A fountain stands in the middle of the park, and Hungarian Wikipedia lists ping-pong tables, a sports ground and two playgrounds among its facilities. Statues and memorials are scattered through the park and on the walls of nearby houses, including memorials to Raoul Wallenberg and to Ferenc Fejtő. The Wallenberg memorial is a sculpture of Saint George fighting a serpent, which a Wallenberg tribute website reads as a symbol of his fight against the Nazis. Its story is told below.

The park gives the neighbourhood a green edge. The decree behind it also asked for the surrounding houses to follow one uniform style, and apartment blocks of five and six storeys now ring the park. At the corner of Pozsonyi út and the park, Hungarian Wikipedia places the Dunapark Kávéház, which it says opened in 1938.

Newer green spaces nearby, among them Duna terasz, Ruttkai Éva park, Thurzó park and Gabriel García Márquez park, were added to take some of the pressure off the park. A city consultation in 2022 gathered proposals for refurbishing the sports facilities and for opening a closed green area on the northern side, so the layout may change; the district and city websites carry the current plans.
tips: Walk to the riverside edge of the park for the view across the Danube to Margaret Island, then continue to the island itself, which has its own page on this site.

Look for the Saint George sculpture and the other memorials; some stand on the walls of houses around the park rather than inside it. Treat the Wallenberg memorial as the place of remembrance that it is, and be considerate when photographing, since this is also a local neighbourhood park.
The Dunapark Kávéház at the corner of Pozsonyi út opened in 1938 according to Hungarian Wikipedia; check its current status before planning a stop.
Check the district or city websites for works or fenced areas before you go.
The apartment blocks around the park follow the uniform style the 1928 decree required, so the streets beside it make an easy short walk.

history.intro: The park is a product of interwar city planning, and its best-known monument has a history of removal and return.

sections.heading: A park on the parquet factory site
paragraphs: The park goes back to a decision of the capital’s public works council in 1928 to lay out a green space on the site of a former parquet factory. Béla Rerrich designed it, and it took shape in 1934–1935. The same decree asked for the houses around it to follow a uniform style at five or six storeys. The park was first called Lipótvárosi park and then Rakovszky park, after the man who had the idea for it, and it has carried the name Szent István since 1937.

Later rebuilds followed in 1961 and 1974, and the most recent major renovation, in 1997–1998, renewed the paths, planting, furniture and playgrounds. The city’s park company, Főkert, planted a rose garden in 2010.

sections.heading: Raoul Wallenberg and the Saint George statue
paragraphs: From July 1944 Raoul Wallenberg, a Swedish diplomat, helped Budapest’s Jews with protective passes and with houses placed under Swedish protection. He was summoned to Soviet headquarters in Debrecen on 17 January 1945 and disappeared that day. Raoul Wallenberg utca in the thirteenth district has carried his name since 1945, and the so-called Swedish houses stood in this district in 1944–1945.

According to the Wallenberg tribute website, the sculptor Pál Pátzay made a Saint George fighting a serpent in Wallenberg’s honour for this park, dated 10 April 1949. It was removed before it could be unveiled; the tribute website records it as having been taken to Debrecen. A full-size replica based on Pátzay’s work, made by Sándor Győrfi, was set up in the original place on 18 April 1999 at the initiative of the Wallenberg Statue Committee. Hungarian Wikipedia’s article on the park mentions the Wallenberg memorial but gives no date or sculptor, so these details rest on the tribute website alone.

name: Erzsébet Square and the Danubius Fountain
address: Erzsébet tér, Budapest V (between Bajcsy-Zsilinszky út and Bécsi utca)
intro: Erzsébet tér is a green square in the middle of Pest’s Inner City, between Bajcsy-Zsilinszky út and Bécsi utca. Its centrepiece is the neo-Renaissance Danubius Fountain, designed by Miklós Ybl and Béla Brestyánszky and built in 1880–1883, which the heritage register says was moved here from Kálvin tér in 1957–1958.
about: Erzsébet tér is a public square and park in District V, in the centre of Pest. Over the years it has been a cemetery, a market, a garden and a bus station site. At its centre stands the Danubius Fountain, which is a listed monument.

The heritage register describes the fountain as a freestanding, multi-tiered structure with a six-lobed lower basin on steps. Allegorical female figures on the plinth stand for three Hungarian rivers, the Tisza, the Dráva and the Száva, and a figure of Danubius on a dolphin crowns the top.

Around the fountain stand the former bus station building, designed by István Nyiri and built in 1948–1949, and a large Ferris wheel, which Hungarian Wikipedia says has stood on the square since the summer of 2013. The bus station building has had monument protection since 1977 and housed the Design Terminal in 2011–2016. Check what play and sports facilities are open on the square before you go.
The square is a natural pause on a walk through downtown Pest. Deák tér, Vörösmarty tér and St Stephen’s Basilica all have their own pages on this site.
tips: Walk all the way round the fountain to find the three river figures and the Danubius figure on the dolphin that the heritage register describes; the masks and shells on the wall basins are easy to miss from a distance.
The former bus station building is a protected monument but its tenants have changed over the years, from the Design Terminal to other uses. Check what is there now before planning around it.
The square makes a good break between the Deák tér area and the Basilica, and Vörösmarty tér is within easy reach; all three have their own pages here.
The heritage register page is a useful reference for the fountain’s details, including the original inscription.
For the Ferris wheel and the venues around the square, use the operators’ own pages for current information rather than relying on older guides.

history.intro: The square’s story runs from a burial ground and market to a public garden, and on to a bus station and a recent park.

sections.heading: From cemetery and market to garden
paragraphs: A welovebudapest history says the site was a cemetery in the seventeenth century and was later turned into a marketplace. Hungarian Wikipedia adds that the ground outside the Váci gate of Pest’s city walls was known first as Új tér and later as Vásártér. The two sources also touch on the square’s name differently: Hungarian Wikipedia dates the name Erzsébet tér to 1858, while welovebudapest mentions an iron fence in 1872 and calls it the first public square named after Empress Elisabeth.

Work on turning the site into a park began in 1854, according to welovebudapest, and by 1870 a Neo-Renaissance kiosk with a café stood there. In 1907 that building was converted into an Art Nouveau house for the National Salon, which was demolished in 1960; Hungarian Wikipedia says only that it came down after the Second World War.

sections.heading: The Danubius Fountain
paragraphs: The heritage register dates the fountain to 1880–1883 and names Miklós Ybl and Béla Brestyánszky as its architects. It says the fountain was moved from Kálvin tér to its present site in 1957–1958. The lower basin once carried a cartouche inscription naming the Pesti Hazai Első Takarékpénztár Egyesület, a savings association, as the donor to the capital, with the years 1880–1883.

Hungarian Wikipedia tells the story differently, saying that the fountain in the middle of the square replaced an original at Kálvin tér that was destroyed in the Second World War. This page follows the heritage register’s account of a move and does not try to settle the difference.

sections.heading: Bus station, theatre pit and park
paragraphs: A bus station was built on the square in 1948–1949, and the welovebudapest article calls it the country’s largest. Hungarian Wikipedia says its traffic moved to the Népliget bus station when that opened in 2002. In 1998 work began on a National Theatre building on the square, but it stopped the same year for lack of funds, and the pit became the Gödör cultural centre in 2002. The Gödör moved to Király utca in 2012, and the Akvárium Klub became a well-known nightlife venue on the square.
The park was renovated in 2006.

name: Vérmező and the Hungarian Jacobins' Memorial Stone
address: Vérmező park, Krisztinaváros (western foot of Castle Hill), Budapest I
intro: Vérmező, the Blood Meadow, is a wide park at the western foot of Castle Hill in Krisztinaváros, Budapest’s first district. Its name recalls the execution of Ignác Martinovics and other leaders of the Hungarian Jacobin conspiracy on 20 May 1795. A coffin-shaped memorial stone by Frigyes Matzon, unveiled in 1955, marks the event.
about: Vérmező is a public park in Krisztinaváros, District I, at the western foot of Várhegy, Castle Hill. Hungarian Wikipedia gives its boundaries as Attila út, Krisztina körút and Mikó utca, and says the Ördög-árok stream runs beneath it.

The memorial to the Hungarian Jacobins is Frigyes Matzon’s coffin-shaped stone, unveiled in 1955, the 160th anniversary of the executions, at the end of the park nearest Széll Kálmán tér. Its inscription names five leaders of the movement: Ignác Martinovics, Ferenc Szentmarjai, József Hajnóczy, János Lackovics and Jakab Sigray. Two further men, Pál Őz and Sándor Szolartsik, are named on it as well.

Several other works stand in the park, according to Hungarian Wikipedia: a memorial to the Buda Volunteer Regiment from 1967 by István Szabó, István Kiss’s dragonfly composition Szitakötők from 1979 near the Mikó utca playground, a reclining figure from 1984 by István János Nagy, and a 2008 statue of the poet Mihály Babits by László Marton, the first public statue of Babits in Budapest.

The park links the Castle District with the streets of Krisztinaváros, and Hungarian Wikipedia sees it as part of a green corridor that brings air from the Buda hills towards the Danube. Residents walk, rest and play here, so a visit is best treated as part of a stroll rather than a stop in itself.
tips: Look for the memorial stone at the end of the park towards Széll Kálmán tér. It is a coffin-shaped block of stone, so read the inscription to understand what it commemorates.
Treat the stone as a memorial to men who were executed: a short pause is more appropriate than posing for photographs on it.
Combine the park with a walk up Castle Hill; the Buda Castle District has its own page on this site, and the Vienna Gate is within reach.
The Kun Béla memorial that once stood at the northern end of the park was moved in 1991 to the sculpture park at Nagytétény, today’s Memento Park, which has its own page on this site.
Check the district municipality’s website for works, events or temporary closures in the park.

history.intro: For centuries the meadow was kept free of buildings below the castle, and in 1795 it became the site of one of Hungary’s best-known political executions.

sections.heading: Open ground below the castle
paragraphs: The meadow began as defensive open ground. A military protection zone was declared at musket-shot distance from the castle walls in 1752, and building on it was banned. By 1784 the governing council had abolished this glacis and was offering plots free to anyone willing to build. In practice the castle used the land as a hayfield, and in the nineteenth century it served as a military training ground. Hungarian Wikipedia says the meadow took roughly its present form in 1830–1833, when roads were rebuilt and the Ördög-árok stream was vaulted over, and that a Millennium military parade and folk festival were held here in 1896.

sections.heading: The Jacobin executions of 1795
paragraphs: Ignác Martinovics and the other leaders of the Hungarian Jacobin conspiracy were executed here on 20 May 1795. That is the date given by Hungarian and English Wikipedia and by the Vérmező section of the First District municipality’s page; one passage on the district page gives 20 March, which contradicts the rest of that page and both Wikipedias. The municipality says the name Vérmező, the Blood Meadow, still recalls the executions.

sections.heading: Rubble, planting and monuments
paragraphs: During the siege of Budapest the meadow was, according to Hungarian Wikipedia, the last place where light courier aircraft could land. After the war the grassy basin was filled with rubble from Castle Hill, and the park was replanted from 1948.

Imre Varga’s multi-figure memorial to Béla Kun was unveiled at the northern end in 1986 and dismantled in 1991, when it was taken to Memento Park. The Matzon stone of 1955 is the memorial to the executions.

seo.description: Vérmező, the Blood Meadow below Castle Hill: where Martinovics and the Hungarian Jacobin leaders were executed in 1795, and its memorials.

name: Óbuda Island (Hajógyári Island)
address: Óbudai-sziget, Budapest III (reached from Óbuda by the K-bridge)
intro: Budapest’s Óbudai-sziget, better known as Hajógyári-sziget or Shipyard Island, is a Danube island of 108 hectares in Budapest’s third district, reached from Óbuda by the K-bridge. A shipyard worked here for more than a century. Today it is a recreation area and the home of the Sziget Festival every August.
about: Óbuda Island lies in the Danube in Budapest’s third district. Hungarian Wikipedia puts the island at 108 hectares and 2,750 metres long. A branch of the river roughly 70–80 metres wide separates it from Óbuda, and the Árpád Bridge passes over its southern end. The everyday name Hajógyári-sziget, Shipyard Island, comes from the shipyard that once worked at that southern end.

Today most of the island is a recreation park with ornamental shrubs and flowers. The former shipyard buildings house offices, warehouses and a yacht club, and the Magyar Yacht Klub operates from the harbour. The city’s planning page treats the island’s established dog walking as a value to preserve, and says the park areas belong to the Budapest Capital Municipality, while the built-up southern and western areas belong to the Hungarian State.

The island also has a natural side. Hungarian Wikipedia reports a strip of soft-wood floodplain forest with white willows and black poplars about 200 years old, and calls the northern tip a stopover for migrating waterbirds. It adds that the capital’s assembly has declared the floodplain forest a locally significant nature reserve.

A visit depends on timing. The city’s 2021–22 consultation described the southern part as closed to the public and proposed opening it and linking it by bus; check what is open now. The Sziget Festival brings large crowds in August and can change access to the island, so check the official sites before travelling.
tips: Walk or cycle over the K-bridge from Óbuda; Hungarian Wikipedia says a bus line, number 226, uses it on weekends in the warmer part of the year, but check the current BKK information before relying on it.
Check the island’s access arrangements around the Sziget Festival in August; the build-up and the festival itself can restrict or change access.

The riverside floodplain woodland and the northern tip, a stopover for migrating waterbirds, are the natural highlights; keep to paths and be considerate of wildlife, which the city plan says it wants to protect.
The city’s 2021–22 consultation described the southern part of the island as closed to the public, so do not plan a route there without checking the current situation.
Combine the island with Óbuda’s Fő tér and the Aquincum Museum, both of which have their own pages on this site.

history.intro: The island’s history runs from Roman-era traces to a shipyard and then to leisure use.

sections.heading: From sandbar to shipyard
paragraphs: The island began as a sandbar formed from two nearby parts, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The Óbuda district page says the Romans already made use of the place, and Hungarian Wikipedia adds that the remains of a palace associated with Hadrian were found on the former shipyard site and still await excavation.

A district library lecture notice dates the shipyard to 1835–1991. English Wikipedia credits Count István Széchenyi with founding it and gives 1836 for the launch of its first ship, the steamboat Árpád. The yard covered 28 hectares, and the rest of the island was farmland.

sections.heading: Parks and the festival
paragraphs: English Wikipedia says May the 9th Park was created in 1973 to mark the centenary of the union of Óbuda, Pest and Buda. The Sziget Festival began in 1993 as Diáksziget, the Students’ Island, and took its present name in 2002; Hungarian Wikipedia says it has been held on the island every August since 1993.
A large hotel and entertainment complex was planned for the island, but English Wikipedia says the project failed in 2013 and the government bought the land back.

sections.heading: The city’s plan for the island
paragraphs: Since early 2020 the city has run a planning process for the island, with a questionnaire that drew about 1,600 respondents, draft plans and on-site meetings. The strategic plan that came out of it puts protecting natural values and biodiversity first and proposes less parking, better park infrastructure, and opening the southern area. It also includes renovation of the K-bridge and coordination with the festival organisers to reduce the festival’s impact on protected areas.

seo.description: Óbuda Island, the Danube's Shipyard Island in Budapest: its history from shipyard to recreation area and Sziget Festival, and the city's plans for it.

name: Buda Capuchin Church
intro: The Buda Capuchin Church on Fő utca, beside Corvin tér, is the parish church of Alsóviziváros, dedicated to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary. It stands on the site of an Ottoman mosque, and its present Romantic exterior dates from the 1850s. The parish history, citing a 2007 yearbook, records that the Capuchin friars again run the parish.
about: The Budai kapucinus templom is the parish church of the Alsóvizivárosi Szent Erzsébet parish, dedicated to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary. It stands at Fő utca 32 near Corvin tér in District I, and the heritage register lists it under the addresses Fő utca 30–32, Corvin János tér 14 and Ponty utca 1–3. It is a protected monument, and the parish history, citing a 2007 yearbook, records that the Capuchins again run the parish.

Hungarian Wikipedia describes a nineteenth-century Romantic historicist exterior that mixes Romanesque and Gothic forms. On the east façade, a central entrance and a triple window are accompanied by reliefs of Saint Stephen and Saint Ladislaus and by a stepped gable framed with octagonal pillars and spires. The tower stands forward of the entrance, and above the door is a statue of Saint Elizabeth by János Marschalkó, dated 1856.

Inside, a nave of four barrel-vaulted bays leads to a narrower choir, and János Garay’s organ stands in the west gallery. The main altar is from 1760 and its altarpiece from 1954. The baroque pews, which Hungarian Wikipedia says came from the Matthias Church in 1876, were restored in 2018 according to the parish.
The former monastery beside the church is a separate property, which Hungarian Wikipedia says has housed a hotel since 2019.
tips: This is a working parish church. Dress and behave as in any place of worship, keep your voice low and avoid photographing during services; check the parish website for service and visiting arrangements.
A section of Ottoman-period wall with two ogee-arched openings is displayed on the south side, and a Turkish wall fragment can be seen inside, according to the parish’s description.
Do not confuse this church with the nearby Saint Anne church on Batthyány tér; the Capuchin church is on Fő utca by Corvin tér.
The Romantic façade and tower are easiest to appreciate from across the street; a wide lens helps on a narrow pavement.
Chain Bridge and Clark Ádám tér are close to Corvin tér and both have their own pages here, making an easy combined walk.

history.intro: The church grew out of an Ottoman mosque, took on its Baroque form in the eighteenth century and was rebuilt in the 1850s in the form seen today.

sections.heading: From mosque to Capuchin church
paragraphs: The parish history says the site already held a building in the Middle Ages, probably an Augustinian friary. In the Ottoman period it carried the mosque of Tojgun Pasha, first mentioned in 1555 and described as a square building under a dome, with a minaret and a Turkish bath nearby. After Buda was retaken in 1686 the Jesuits received the mosque in 1687 and used it as a parish church. In the same year György Széchényi, Archbishop of Esztergom and Prince-Primate, founded a Capuchin monastery in Buda.
The friars took over the buildings in 1692, converted the temporary church, and had it consecrated to Saint Elizabeth of Hungary on 20 September 1716.

sections.heading: Baroque additions and the nineteenth-century rebuilding
paragraphs: A main altar of 1760, paid for by Countess Erzsébet Bercsényi, widow of Count Miklós Zichy, and an eastern extension of 1776–1777 with a volute-gabled façade shaped the Baroque church; Joseph II restored its parish status in 1787. After damage in the siege of 1849 the church was rebuilt in 1854–1856 under the National Building Directorate, led by Ferenc Reitter, in a round-arched style with Gothic Revival elements. It was consecrated on 22 November 1856, and the heritage register credits the façade to Reitter and Gerster.

sections.heading: War damage and return of the friars
paragraphs: The interior was renovated in 1926–1927. In 1944–1945 a bomb destroyed much of the eighteenth-century furnishings and wall painting, and the interior was restored after the war. The parish says the Capuchin order was dissolved after the war, and Hungarian Wikipedia says the monastery was nationalised in 1950. The exterior was renovated in 1968–1969.
